narrative:
The model estimates a 49% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution against investing in someone who might soon depart.

The decision was driven primarily by three key factors. First, the number of training programs you attended over the past three years had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward you staying. You completed seven or more programs, far more than most employees the model expected to remain (only 19% of stayers had this level). This strong positive signal was, however, outweighed by the next two factors.

Second, having received other job offers while at the company was the most powerful reason the model leaned toward you leaving. This is relatively uncommon—only 23% of predicted stayers had outside opportunities—suggesting the model sees this as a clear sign you may be considering alternatives.

Third, the length of time you have spent in your current role also pulled the prediction toward staying. Your 6–10 years here is longer than most stayers (51% have only 1–5 years), indicating loyalty that the model recognizes.

Overall, your external opportunities created enough concern to tip the balance. The organization should discuss your career goals openly with you and explore whether additional responsibilities or changes could reduce the appeal of outside offers. You, in turn, may want to reflect on what would make staying the clear first choice. (248 words)
